fixes.explanation: No chains in this story. Jacob says, “…surely by now you would have sent me away empty-handed.” (Genesis 31:42). He points to the God of his father being with him as the reason that didn't happen. Chains would make for a much scarier speech, but empty hands is what he actually says.

No tower here, friend. The relatives “…took stones and made a mound…” (Genesis 31:46). Jacob had also set up one stone as a pillar (Genesis 31:45). A tower would need a lot more stacking, and I know about heavy lifting, because I once got carried across a kitchen by one shiny new stamper's owner.

It's true, baker. Laban says, “If you mistreat my daughters or take other wives, although no one is with us, remember that God is a witness between you and me.” (Genesis 31:50). Even with no one else around, God is a witness. Laban puts that right in the agreement.

It happens, baker. The text says, “Early the next morning, Laban got up and kissed his grandchildren and daughters and blessed them.” (Genesis 31:55). Back in verse 28 he complained that Jacob didn't let him kiss them goodbye. Now he gets to, and then he heads home.

No guard in his offer, friend. Laban talks about music: “…with joy and singing, with tambourines and harps.” (Genesis 31:27). Picture a send-off with tambourines and harps. That's a parade, not a security detail.

Laban says the opposite, baker. He tells Jacob, “I have power to do you great harm…” (Genesis 31:29). Then he says that last night the God of Jacob's father told him, “Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad.” (Genesis 31:29). He has the power, and he tells Jacob about the warning.

Silver, baker? Nope, nobody mentions a single coin. Laban asks, “But why have you stolen my gods?” (Genesis 31:30). He's chased Jacob for seven days and the thing he's after isn't money at all. I've lost things in a junk drawer, but I never chased anybody for seven days over it.

Laban goes through Jacob's tent, Leah's tent and the tents of the two maidservants, and “…he found nothing.” (Genesis 31:33). Leah is Rachel's sister and Jacob's wife. That's four tents and zero idols, with one more tent still to go.

Sold? Not a word about it, baker. Jacob says, “…nor have I eaten the rams of your flock.” (Genesis 31:38). He's telling Laban he didn't eat any of the rams. It's a short line, but he's making a point after twenty years of work.

A home of his own? Nice thought, but Jacob doesn't say it. He says he served “…fourteen years for your two daughters…” (Genesis 31:41). The other six years were “for your flocks.” (Genesis 31:41). That's the full breakdown he gives Laban.

Laban doesn't ask Jacob to come back with him, friend. He says, “Come now, let us make a covenant, you and I…” (Genesis 31:44). He wants an agreement between the two of them. Jacob never gets a ride home with him.

Jacob tells his relatives, “Gather some stones.” They “…took stones and made a mound…” (Genesis 31:46). Before that, Jacob had set up one stone as a pillar (Genesis 31:45). Then they ate there by the mound. A stone pile with a dinner table, I like it.

Grave? That's a gloomy guess, baker. Laban says, “This mound is a witness between you and me this day.” (Genesis 31:48). The text calls it a witness and says nothing about a burial. Keep your eyes on the word witness.

Laban says it goes both ways. He says, “…I will not go past this mound to harm you, and you will not go past this mound and pillar to harm me.” (Genesis 31:52). Both men promise not to pass the stones to harm the other. Jacob is no more free to harm Laban than Laban is to harm him.
Right, baker. After they ate, “…they spent the night on the mountain.” (Genesis 31:54). Laban left “Early the next morning…” (Genesis 31:55). So he stayed the night and left at daybreak.
